CONFIDENCE: 88

Yes. Absolute productivity advantages do not rule out mutual gains. What matters is comparative advantage: each country should specialize in the good for which its opportunity cost is lower, then trade. Even if A produces both cars and wheat more efficiently than B, the ratio of those productivities will generally differ, so one country’s relative cost of cars (in forgone wheat) will be lower than the other’s. Specializing along those lines and exchanging at a price between the two autarky price ratios lets both consume more of both goods than they could alone.

CONFIDENCE: 95

A binding price ceiling (maximum legal rent set below the market-clearing rent) produces a shortage of apartments. At that lower price, quantity demanded rises while quantity supplied falls, so more households want units than landlords are willing to offer.

CONFIDENCE: 95

Empirical labor-economics research finds that immigration has little to no large negative effect on the wages of native-born low-skilled workers. Estimates from natural experiments (such as the Mariel boatlift), cross-city and national panel studies, and the 2017 National Academies of Sciences review typically range from roughly zero to small declines of a few percent, concentrated among prior immigrants and native high-school dropouts; some studies find small positive effects via complementarity and task specialization. Disagreement remains (notably Borjas versus Card/Peri), but the weight of evidence does not support large wage reductions for natives.

CONFIDENCE: 82

Yes. Phasing out leaded gasoline and restricting lead paint produced large, well-documented net benefits.

Lead is a potent neurotoxin with no safe exposure level, especially for young children. Before regulation, average U.S. childhood blood-lead levels were roughly 15 µg/dL; after the gasoline phase-out (largely complete by the mid-1990s) and the 1978 residential paint ban, they fell below 1 µg/dL. That decline tracks the removal of the dominant exposure sources and is observed across countries that took similar steps.

The health gains are not speculative. Lower lead exposure is causally linked to higher cognitive scores, fewer behavioral and cardiovascular problems, and reduced premature mortality. Economic valuations of the IQ and productivity effects alone—using standard dose-response estimates and lifetime earnings—run into the hundreds of billions of dollars in the United States, far exceeding the compliance costs of reformulated gasoline, catalytic converters, and paint substitution. Crime reductions associated with the same cohort exposure drop, while still debated in magnitude, point in the same direction and are not required for the net-benefit conclusion.

Residual lead in soil and old housing remains a problem, and abatement is incomplete, but that does not reverse the historical accounting: the regulations removed the largest ongoing sources of population exposure at a cost much smaller than the harms they prevented.

CONFIDENCE: 92

No. Lead use in U.S. household paint was already declining well before the 1978 CPSC residential ban (which set a 0.06% limit). Industry voluntary limits (about 1% for interior paint) date to the mid-1950s, titanium-dioxide pigments displaced much lead earlier, and the 1971 Lead-Based Paint Poisoning Prevention Act already restricted lead paint in federally assisted housing. Housing surveys reflect that decline: lead paint is far more common in pre-1940 and 1940–1959 homes than in 1960–1978 homes. The 1978 rule largely finished a phase-out already under way rather than starting it.

CONFIDENCE: 88

No. Large pay differences are not inherently unfair.

Pay largely tracks differences in scarce skills, responsibility, hours, risk, and the value others voluntarily place on someone’s output. A surgeon, founder, or specialist whose work creates far more measurable value—or who bears far more downside—can reasonably earn many times what a less specialized role pays, even when both people “work.” Equal pay for unequal contribution is itself a fairness problem. Market wages are imperfect (luck, bargaining power, discrimination, and rents all matter), so some gaps are unjustified and worth correcting through open competition, better education, and rules against fraud or coercion. But a 50-to-1 ratio, by itself, does not prove unfairness; what matters is whether the gap comes from voluntary exchange and real differences in contribution, or from privilege and blocked opportunity.

CONFIDENCE: 72

No. Signature literacy (the standard historical proxy) was already widespread and rising for decades before state elementary schooling became significant. Around 1840 roughly two-thirds of men and half of women in England and Wales could sign the marriage register; by the 1870 Forster Act those figures were about 80% and 73%. Near-universal literacy followed later, but the main rise to mass levels occurred under voluntary, private, charity, and Sunday schools, not under compulsion or state provision (attendance made compulsory only in 1880; fees ended in 1891).

CONFIDENCE: 82

Cities that introduced congestion pricing have generally found substantial drops in traffic volumes and congestion inside the charged zones (often on the order of 15–30%), faster and more reliable travel times, shifts toward public transit, modest air-quality gains, and net revenue that can fund transport improvements. Public opposition commonly softens once the benefits are visible.

CONFIDENCE: 85

The corporate income tax is legally paid by corporations, but its economic incidence (who is made worse off) is not confined to them. In standard public-finance analysis the tax reduces the after-tax return to corporate capital. Capital then reallocates toward the non-corporate sector and, in an open economy, toward lower-tax jurisdictions. The resulting decline in the domestic capital stock lowers labor productivity and therefore wages, so part of the burden is shifted to workers. A smaller share may also appear as higher consumer prices when firms have market power.

Quantitative estimates of the labor share vary with modeling assumptions (capital mobility, time horizon, country size) and with the empirical strategy employed; official scoring conventions commonly assign roughly one-quarter of the burden to labor and the rest to owners of capital, while some studies find a larger labor share. The robust conclusion is that the burden is shared between capital owners and workers rather than resting solely on corporate shareholders or on the firms that remit the tax.

CONFIDENCE: 78

Empirical research on city- and state-level minimum-wage hikes of roughly 10–15% finds that overall employment (and low-wage employment in particular) changes very little. Estimated employment elasticities cluster near zero; any disemployment that appears is typically small, concentrated among the least-experienced workers, and often offset by higher hourly earnings for those who remain employed. Larger or more rapid increases can produce clearer hour and job reductions, but that is outside the moderate range specified here.

CONFIDENCE: 68

Yes. The clearest U.S. case is thalidomide in 1960–61. Under the 1938 Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act’s pre-market safety requirement, FDA medical officer Frances Kelsey repeatedly refused to approve Richardson-Merrell’s application because the safety data were inadequate (including on pregnancy). The drug was already widely sold in Europe and elsewhere and caused thousands of severe birth defects; it was never approved for U.S. sale. Only a small number of U.S. cases occurred from investigational samples. Contemporary and historical accounts treat that non-approval as having prevented a large-scale U.S. tragedy, and the episode helped drive the 1962 Kefauver–Harris Amendments.

CONFIDENCE: 88

No. Multinational factories in poor countries generally pay well above local alternatives (often several times prevailing wages in agriculture or informal work), which is why workers compete for those jobs. Boycotts that shut plants or cut orders typically push people into worse options and do not raise their living standards.

The pattern is consistent across apparel, electronics, and similar export sectors: foreign firms pay premiums relative to domestic employers, wages exceed legal minima where those exist, and measured consumption and health outcomes for factory households are better than for non-factory peers in the same regions. Workers accept the conditions because the outside option—subsistence farming, street vending, or domestic service—is poorer in pay, safety, and stability. When campaigns or buyer pull-outs close factories, employment falls and former workers report lower earnings and more hazardous informal work; child-labor bans imposed from outside have sometimes shifted children into worse activities rather than school. Raising productivity and local labor demand, not reducing demand for the jobs people already prefer, is what improves wages over time.

CONFIDENCE: 85

No. Within-group heritability only describes how much of the variation *inside* each group is associated with genetic differences among its members. It does not identify the causes of a difference in group means.

A trait can be highly heritable within each of two groups while the entire gap between their averages is environmental. Standard illustrations include height (strongly heritable, yet secular increases are nutritional) and genetically identical seed stocks grown in different soils (within-plot heritability can be high while the between-plot difference is wholly environmental). The same logic applies to IQ: substantial heritability within groups is compatible with a between-group gap that is partly genetic, wholly environmental, or any mixture; the heritability figures alone do not distinguish those possibilities.

CONFIDENCE: 92

Occupational licensing (government-mandated entry requirements such as training hours, exams, and fees) has been studied extensively in labor economics. The main documented effects, especially for lower-risk occupations such as barbers, cosmetologists, florists, and many contractor trades, are:

- **Restricted labor supply and higher practitioner earnings.** Requirements reduce entry. Licensed workers earn a wage premium on the order of 10–15% relative to similar unlicensed workers (Kleiner, Krueger, and related studies; White House/CEA summaries of the literature).
- **Higher consumer prices.** The supply restriction and wage premium are passed through as higher prices for services, with little offsetting evidence of large quality gains in the cited occupations.
- **Weak or null quality/safety effects in many cases.** For barbering, cosmetology, floristry, and similar fields, studies generally find little or no measurable improvement in outcomes, complaints, or safety that would justify the stringency of the rules. Effects are more plausible (though still often poorly measured) in higher-stakes trades.
- **Lower geographic mobility.** Because rules differ sharply across states and are often non-transferable, licensing reduces interstate migration of workers in licensed occupations.
- **Distributional barriers.** The fixed costs of compliance fall harder on lower-income people, career-switchers, immigrants, and some minority groups, reducing their access to these jobs.

Net, the empirical literature finds clear costs in prices, employment, and mobility, with benefits that are small or undocumented for many of the occupations in the question’s examples. Results vary by occupation and by how strict the rules are; high-risk fields (e.g., medicine, electrical work) are a partial exception where some consumer-protection rationale is stronger.

CONFIDENCE: 82

Yes. Vaccination often generates positive externalities that private decisions underprovide, so subsidies (and sometimes requirements) can raise social welfare on standard economic grounds, not only medical ones.

When a person is vaccinated they capture private benefits (lower personal risk of illness, medical bills, and lost earnings) but also confer unpriced benefits on others: less transmission, protection of people who cannot be vaccinated, lower strain on shared health systems, and fewer workplace and school disruptions. Herd immunity is a classic public good with free-rider incentives. Because the social marginal benefit exceeds the private marginal benefit, an unsubsidized market tends to vaccinate too little relative to the social optimum. A Pigouvian subsidy equal to the external benefit, or a requirement that achieves a similar coverage level at acceptable cost, can close that gap.

Empirical work on diseases with meaningful transmission reduction (measles, pertussis, influenza, and others) routinely finds that the social return—avoided treatment costs, productivity losses, and outbreak externalities—exceeds private willingness to pay and often exceeds program cost by a wide margin. The case is weaker when a product mainly reduces severity in the recipient and barely blocks spread, or when side-effect and administrative costs are high; it is stronger when coverage externalities are large and the alternative is repeated outbreaks. Mandates are a blunter instrument than subsidies or targeted incentives and impose liberty and enforcement costs, but they remain an economically coherent response when free-riding would otherwise leave coverage below the threshold that protects the unvaccinated and when subsidies alone cannot reach it.

Thus the economic rationale is market failure from externalities and public goods, plus fiscal and productivity spillovers—not merely individual clinical benefit.

CONFIDENCE: 88

Personality traits such as extraversion and neuroticism are moderately heritable. Twin, family, and adoption studies consistently attribute roughly 40–60% of the observed individual differences in these traits to genetic factors (with meta-analytic averages often near 40–50%). The remaining variance is explained mainly by non-shared environmental influences; shared family environment contributes little. Molecular (SNP-based) estimates are lower, reflecting many small-effect variants and the limits of current genomic methods rather than a contradiction of the twin-study results.

CONFIDENCE: 88

Yes. The Montreal Protocol (1987, with later amendments) phased out the bulk of CFC and related ozone-depleting production and consumption. Atmospheric abundances of the main CFCs peaked and have since declined; the Antarctic ozone hole has stopped worsening and is slowly healing, with full recovery of mid-latitude and polar ozone expected around mid-century if compliance holds. That outcome is measured, not merely modeled: ground and satellite records show both the chemical decline and the ozone response.

A treaty was required because stratospheric ozone is a global commons. CFCs are long-lived and well mixed, so emissions anywhere thin the ozone layer everywhere; one country’s unilateral ban would not protect its own population and would put its industries at a cost disadvantage. Coordinated phase-outs, trade restrictions on non-parties, and a science-based adjustment mechanism solved the free-rider problem and gave firms a clear signal to switch to substitutes.

CONFIDENCE: 92

Yes. Large, replicated average sex differences in occupational interests are a well-established finding in vocational psychology, especially on the people–things dimension.

Meta-analyses of interest inventories (notably Su, Rounds & Armstrong, 2009, covering dozens of samples and hundreds of thousands of people, using Holland’s RIASEC framework and Prediger’s people–things axis) find:

- Men score substantially higher on “things” / Realistic interests and women on “people” / Social interests.
- The bipolar people–things contrast shows an effect size of about *d* ≈ 0.9–1.0 (men more thing-oriented). That is a large difference by conventional benchmarks—one of the largest average sex differences in psychology—while still leaving substantial overlap between the distributions.
- Related contrasts are smaller but directionally consistent (e.g., men higher on Realistic, women higher on Social and, to a lesser extent, Artistic/Conventional).

These patterns appear across decades, assessment methods, and many countries; they emerge by adolescence and are not an artifact of a single instrument. Magnitude can vary somewhat by culture and cohort, but the direction and the large size of the people–things gap are robust. The finding is descriptive of averages, not a claim that every individual matches the group pattern or that the causes are fully settled.

CONFIDENCE: 90

Mass child labor (especially industrial) fell sharply in the US well before effective nationwide bans. Census and labor-force data show employment of children aged 10–15 dropping from roughly 18% around 1900 to well under 5% by 1930—before the Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938. State age, hour, and schooling statutes of the Progressive Era contributed in some sectors and accelerated the trend where they were enforced, but quantitative work (e.g., Moehling and related economic-history studies) finds they explain only a minority of the decline. The larger drivers were rising adult real wages and family incomes, which reduced the need for children’s earnings, together with technological and sectoral change that lowered demand for unskilled juvenile labor and raised the return to schooling.

CONFIDENCE: 62

The Federal Reserve was created by the Federal Reserve Act of 1913, primarily in response to repeated banking panics (especially 1907) under the prior National Banking System. Those crises featured sudden liquidity shortages, bank runs, and contractions with no central lender of last resort or elastic currency. Congress designed the Fed to supply emergency liquidity, supervise banks, and manage the money supply so as to reduce panics and support a more stable payments and credit system. Later statutes (notably the 1977 dual mandate) added explicit goals of maximum employment and stable prices.

On fulfillment, the record is mixed rather than a clear success or failure. Classic nationwide banking panics became far less frequent after the Fed (and after FDIC deposit insurance in 1933) than in the 19th and early 20th centuries. The Fed has repeatedly acted as lender of last resort—in 1987, 2008, and 2020—and those interventions limited immediate systemic collapse. Post-war recessions have also tended to be shorter and milder than many pre-Fed downturns, and long-run inflation has been lower and less volatile since the Volcker disinflation than in the 1970s.

At the same time, the Fed has not eliminated instability and has sometimes amplified it. Monetary contraction in the early 1930s deepened the Great Depression; the 1970s saw a major inflationary failure; and credit booms preceding 2008 and the post-2020 inflation surge reflected policy and regulatory shortcomings as well as private-sector excess. Financial crises, regional bank failures, and large output gaps have continued. Most economic historians therefore treat the Fed as an improvement on the pre-1913 regime for panic prevention, but not as an institution that has reliably stabilized the broader economy.

CONFIDENCE: 72

No. The Great Depression began with the October 1929 stock-market crash and the subsequent contraction in output and credit, well before the Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act was signed in June 1930. The Act raised U.S. import duties sharply and triggered foreign retaliation that further reduced already-falling trade, so it aggravated the slump, but trade was too small a share of the U.S. economy, and the timing is wrong, for the tariff to have been the cause. Mainstream economic history instead emphasizes monetary contraction, banking panics, and the gold standard as the central drivers.

CONFIDENCE: 88

Yes. The 1990 Acid Rain Program’s SO2 cap-and-trade system cut power-plant SO2 emissions far below the statutory cap (from roughly 16 million tons around 1990 to well under half that by the early 2000s, and lower still later), reduced wet sulfate deposition across the eastern United States by on the order of half or more in many areas, and did so at compliance costs well below pre-enactment command-and-control forecasts. Allowance trading and banking functioned as designed; independent evaluations (EPA, NAPAP follow-ups, and economic studies such as Ellerman et al.) find benefits—especially from lower fine-particle exposure—that substantially exceeded costs. Surface-water chemistry improved where sulfate was the main driver, though full ecological recovery of soils, forests, and some lakes has been slower and incomplete because of legacy base-cation depletion and ongoing nitrogen deposition. Those limits qualify the ecological endpoint; they do not overturn the program’s success on emissions, deposition, cost, and health goals.

CONFIDENCE: 90

Standard Oil’s refining market share had already been eroding for years (from roughly 90% in the 1880s–1890s toward the mid-60% range by 1911) under competition from new fields and rivals, while the price of kerosene continued its long decline.

CONFIDENCE: 78

The interwar gold standard was a major propagator and amplifier of the Great Depression. By fixing currencies to gold at set parities, it forced central banks to defend reserves with high interest rates and monetary contraction whenever gold flowed out, transmitting deflation, banking stress, and output collapse across borders instead of allowing independent easing. Countries that suspended convertibility and devalued early (notably Britain and much of Scandinavia in 1931, then the United States in 1933) regained monetary autonomy, expanded money and credit, and saw faster rebounds in prices and industrial production; those that stayed on gold longer (the gold bloc) endured deeper and more prolonged slumps.

CONFIDENCE: 88

Yes. Smallpox eradication was a clear success of coordinated public action, and it is not plausible that ordinary market activity alone would have achieved it.

The disease was declared eradicated in 1980 after the last natural case in 1977. That outcome followed the WHO’s Intensified Smallpox Eradication Programme (from 1967), which combined mass and then ring vaccination, active surveillance, case containment, and cross-border coordination, financed and executed by national governments, the WHO, and public-health agencies such as the CDC. Vaccine technology (Jenner, 1796) had existed for nearly two centuries without producing global eradication; incidence fell in richer countries mainly where states imposed compulsory vaccination and public-health controls, while transmission continued in poorer regions until the coordinated campaign.

Eradication is a global public good: benefits are non-excludable and non-rival, so private buyers and sellers systematically under-provide the last, hardest increments of coverage. Herd immunity creates a free-rider problem; once local risk falls, individual willingness to pay collapses even though pushing incidence to zero still requires universal reach, including people who cannot pay. Markets also do not supply the non-commercial functions the campaign actually used—case finding, isolation, contact tracing, and enforcement across jurisdictions—nor do they solve the international externality that an endemic focus anywhere threatens everywhere. Pharmaceutical incentives, moreover, favor continued sales over elimination of the market. Historical experience matches the theory: voluntary and commercial vaccination never closed the remaining reservoirs.

Thus coordinated public programs were both what worked and what economic and epidemiological constraints make necessary.

CONFIDENCE: 92

Municipal clean-water technologies (filtration and chlorination) accounted for nearly half of the total mortality decline in major U.S. cities over 1900–1936 (and for roughly three-quarters of the infant-mortality decline and nearly two-thirds of the child-mortality decline). These estimates come from the causal analysis in Cutler & Miller (Demography, 2005), which exploits plausibly exogenous variation in the timing of municipal adoption.

CONFIDENCE: 75

The 1962 Kefauver-Harris Amendments, which created the modern FDA pre-market efficacy (and tightened safety) requirements, produced a large, persistent drop in new drug introductions. Economic estimates of the resulting consumer-welfare loss—from both fewer drugs and multi-year approval lags relative to peer regulators—exceed the gains from keeping ineffective or dangerous compounds off the market.

The clearest quantitative anchor remains Peltzman’s 1973 analysis: roughly a 50–60 % decline in new chemical entities, with the surplus forgone by patients larger than the surplus saved by avoiding useless drugs. Later work on specific lags (beta-blockers, certain AIDS and cancer agents, etc.) finds thousands of excess deaths per delayed therapy; these “invisible graveyard” costs are systematic, not anecdotal. Comparative approval-time data show the United States frequently trailing Europe and Japan without a commensurate safety advantage. Innovation effects compound the problem: higher fixed costs of approval disproportionately suppress drugs for smaller or less profitable indications.

Benefits exist—thalidomide is the canonical case—but they are smaller and less frequent than the cumulative mortality and morbidity from delay and reduced R&D. Post-1962 safety disasters (e.g., Vioxx) further show that pre-market review does not eliminate large risks, while mechanisms such as accelerated approval and Emergency Use Authorization demonstrate that faster pathways can be net beneficial when the alternative is waiting. On standard welfare metrics, therefore, the regime has made Americans worse off.

CONFIDENCE: 62

The “China shock” research (chiefly Autor, Dorn, and Hanson) found that the surge in Chinese imports after China’s WTO entry caused large, geographically concentrated losses of U.S. manufacturing jobs. In exposed local labor markets those losses were not offset by gains in other sectors: employment, labor-force participation, and wages fell, while unemployment and transfer payments (disability, unemployment insurance, etc.) rose, and the adverse effects persisted for a decade or more.

CONFIDENCE: 88

Yes. Federal deposit insurance (FDIC, 1933) ended the pre-1930s pattern of frequent, contagious retail bank runs and panics that amplified downturns into systemic collapses. Bank failure rates and depositor losses fell sharply for decades afterward; the Diamond–Dybvig logic and the historical record both show that credible insurance removes the first-mover incentive that turns illiquidity into insolvency cascades.

Moral hazard is real—insurance dulls depositor monitoring and contributed to risk-taking in the S&L crisis and to runs on uninsured deposits in 2008 and 2023—but those episodes were contained without 1930s-style collapses of the insured deposit base. Premiums, supervision, and resolution powers have been imperfect offsets, yet the net effect on systemic stability has been positive relative to the uninsured era.

CONFIDENCE: 78

No. Heritability is the fraction of observed variation in a trait, within a given population and environment, that is associated with genetic differences. It says nothing about how much the trait’s average level can shift if the environment itself changes. A trait can be highly heritable and still be strongly responsive to environmental change (height is a standard example: highly heritable within populations, yet population means have risen substantially with nutrition and health).

CONFIDENCE: 95

No. The 1999 Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act (which repealed the core affiliation barriers of the 1933 Glass-Steagall Act) was not a cause of the 2008 crisis.

The institutions at the center of the failure—Bear Stearns, Lehman Brothers, Merrill Lynch, AIG, and the government-sponsored enterprises—were not commercial banks whose risky activities had been unlocked by the repeal. Pure investment banks and insurers could already engage in the securitization, proprietary trading, and derivatives activities that blew up; Glass-Steagall had never constrained them. The mortgage bubble, subprime origination (much of it by non-banks), excessive leverage in the shadow-banking system, flawed credit ratings, and housing-policy incentives predated and operated independently of the 1999 law. Large commercial-bank holding companies such as Citigroup had already formed under pre-1999 loopholes; GLBA largely ratified existing practice rather than creating the exposures that later produced losses.

Post-crisis reviews (Financial Crisis Inquiry Commission majority, Fed and Treasury analyses, and the bulk of academic work) identify leverage, liquidity mismatches, housing credit, and risk-management failures as the drivers. Countries without Glass-Steagall-style separations experienced parallel problems, and the activities later restricted by the Volcker Rule were not the binding constraint in 2007–08. The repeal contributed to larger, more diversified financial firms, but that structural change was neither necessary nor sufficient for the crisis.

CONFIDENCE: 82

Randomised evaluations (notably the coordinated set of RCTs in Bosnia, Ethiopia, India, Mexico, Mongolia, Morocco and the Philippines) found that expanding access to microcredit produced only modest, uneven gains in business activity and investment for some borrowers. Average effects on household income, consumption, and broader poverty measures were small and generally statistically indistinguishable from zero, with little consistent evidence of transformative gains in living standards, health, education or women’s empowerment.

CONFIDENCE: 88

Inflation stayed low and stable (generally near or below the Fed’s 2% target) through the 2010s; there was no runaway inflation. The predictions failed because they treated base-money growth as if it would automatically raise spending. In the post-crisis liquidity trap, most of the reserves created by QE sat idle as excess bank reserves (especially once the Fed paid interest on them), broader money grew far more slowly, the velocity of money collapsed amid deleveraging and weak loan demand, and a large output gap plus anchored expectations kept price pressure subdued.

CONFIDENCE: 90

No. Natural resource wealth does not systematically curse economic growth. Early cross-country work (notably Sachs and Warner) found a negative association between resource dependence and growth, but later research shows that result is fragile and highly conditional.

The association weakens or disappears once measurement is improved (abundance versus export dependence; point-source minerals versus diffuse agriculture), institutions and governance are controlled for, and endogeneity is addressed. Resource-rich economies with strong institutions and prudent fiscal rules (Norway, Botswana, Chile, Australia, Canada) have grown at least as fast as peers; many poorly governed exporters have not. Volatility, Dutch-disease effects, and rent-seeking can slow growth, but these are policy and institutional outcomes, not automatic consequences of geology. Meta-analyses and more recent panels therefore treat any “curse” as contingent rather than general.

CONFIDENCE: 78

Twin, adoption, and genomic studies converge on substantial genetic influence on IQ differences among people within a population. Classical twin designs find that identical twins are markedly more similar in IQ than fraternal twins (including when reared apart); heritability is typically estimated around 40–50% in childhood and rises to roughly 60–80% in adulthood. Adoption studies show the same pattern from another angle: by adolescence and adulthood, adoptees’ IQs correlate more strongly with their biological relatives than with the adoptive family that reared them. Genome-wide association studies and related genomic methods confirm a highly polygenic contribution—thousands of common variants of small effect—with SNP-based heritability often in the range of about 20–30% (or somewhat higher with newer methods) and polygenic scores that reliably predict a portion of individual differences, though they still capture only part of the heritability seen in twin and adoption data. Environmental factors also matter, and estimates vary by age, measurement, and population, but the three designs agree that genetic differences are a major source of within-population IQ variation.

CONFIDENCE: 88

Migrant remittances to low- and middle-income countries are substantially larger than official development assistance (ODA). In recent years they have run on the order of three times ODA (roughly $600+ billion versus about $200 billion annually) and have exceeded aid since the late 1990s.

Their economic profiles also differ. Remittances are private household-to-household transfers: relatively stable, often counter-cyclical, and spent mainly on consumption, education, health, and small-scale investment, with no policy conditions attached. ODA is public finance—grants and concessional loans from governments and multilaterals—more volatile, shaped by donor budgets and politics, frequently conditional, and channeled through states or projects toward public goods and budget support, with higher overhead and different leakage risks.

CONFIDENCE: 88

Occupational licensing raises pay for workers who hold the license (typically a wage premium on the order of 10–15 percent in U.S. estimates) by restricting entry and thereby limiting labor supply in the occupation. Because licensing rules differ across states and are often not fully portable, the same requirements reduce workers’ ability to move between states for work, lowering interstate migration rates among licensed occupations.

CONFIDENCE: 82

Taxi medallion systems capped the number of street-hail taxis and made the right to operate a transferable, scarce license. That artificial limit created large scarcity rents: medallions traded as financial assets (often above $1 million in New York around 2013–14), were heavily debt-financed, and protected incumbents while restricting supply, raising fares, and lengthening waits.

Rideshare entry (Uber, Lyft, and similar app dispatch) largely bypassed the cap. The sudden increase in for-hire supply cut prices and wait times for riders and destroyed most of the capitalized value of medallions. Owners who had bought at peak prices absorbed large capital losses; many loans went bad, and some cities later added fees or caps on rideshares partly in response to that collapse.

CONFIDENCE: 88

No. US Prohibition (18th Amendment and Volstead Act, 1920–1933) cut legal alcohol supply and lowered per-capita consumption and some alcohol-related deaths relative to the pre-1920 peak, but it did not achieve its aims of a dry society, better public order, or lasting moral reform, and it was repealed because those failures were obvious.

Consumption of pure alcohol fell sharply at first (commonly estimated on the order of 30–70% below late-1910s levels) and stayed below the pre-Prohibition trend for much of the period; cirrhosis mortality and some alcohol-related admissions also dropped. Drinking did not stop. Illegal production, smuggling, and speakeasies supplied a large black market; consumption rebounded somewhat after the early years; and patterns shifted toward harder liquor. Enforcement was uneven, under-resourced, and widely evaded, especially in cities.

The costs were large and visible: organized crime and gang violence expanded around bootlegging, homicide rates rose in many cities, corruption of police and officials was widespread, and the federal government lost a major tax base just as the Depression hit. Respect for the law eroded. Those effects, not a sudden return to pre-1920 drinking levels, drove repeal in 1933. After repeal, consumption rose again but did not instantly restore the old peak; the policy itself is still judged a failure on its own stated goals.

CONFIDENCE: 78

Official estimates (notably the 2017 National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine report, with supporting federal analyses such as recent CBO budget projections) find that the net fiscal effect is mixed by level of government and generation but modest overall relative to the economy. First-generation immigrants and their dependent children typically impose net costs on state and local budgets (driven largely by education), while contributing positively or less negatively at the federal level; their U.S.-born children are strong net fiscal contributors. Over long horizons the combined effect of immigrants plus descendants is often modestly positive for the federal budget and small in either direction for all levels of government combined, varying with immigrants’ age, education, and labor-market outcomes.

CONFIDENCE: 72

Certificate-of-need (CON) laws restrict entry and expansion, so they reduce the supply of hospitals, beds, imaging equipment, and ambulatory surgery centers relative to non-CON states. By limiting competition they fail to contain costs and are associated with higher prices and spending. They do not raise quality; the evidence is neutral to negative (including worse outcomes for some conditions).

CONFIDENCE: 82

Empirical studies (especially of restaurants and other low-wage sectors) find that a large share of minimum-wage cost increases is passed through to consumer prices—often near-complete pass-through of the affected labor-cost share in the short run. A frequently cited benchmark is that a 10% minimum-wage rise raises restaurant prices by roughly 0.7% (Aaronson, French & MacDonald and related work); other estimates are smaller (on the order of a few tenths of a percent) but still economically meaningful. Economy-wide, pass-through is partial because many firms and sectors employ few minimum-wage workers and some of the cost is absorbed in margins.

Incidence therefore falls mainly on consumers of minimum-wage-intensive goods and services (via higher prices), partly on owners (lower profits), and partly on workers where hours or employment adjust.
